THE PROOF OF BARNETTE’S CONJECTURE: AN EXPOSITION
Abstract. We give a self-contained exposition of OpenAI’s 2026 proof of Barnette’s conjecture, in the
form that every cubic, bipartite, 3-connected planar graph has a Hamiltonian cycle avoiding any given
edge. In a cubic graph the complement of a perfect matching has degree two at every vertex, so the task
is to find a perfect matching whose complement is connected. In the planar dual, a triangulation whose
triangles are coloured black and white, a perfect matching corresponds to a set of edges containing
exactly one side of every triangle; the matching’s complement in the original graph is connected exactly
when this set contains no cycle. We reduce the search for such a set to a choice of one corner in each
black triangle. A suitable choice exists because of a signed count over pairs of choices, in which the
unsuitable ones cancel and a second grouping of the same sum shows that it is not zero. The avoided
edge is what lets an induction cut the triangulation along triangles that are not faces.
1. Introduction
A Hamiltonian cycle is a connected spanning subgraph in which every vertex has degree two. In a cubic
graph the degree condition is the easy half. Deleting a perfect matching leaves every vertex with two
edges, and a cubic bipartite graph has a perfect matching by Hall’s theorem. Connectivity is the whole
problem. On the cube, the two opposite squares form a subgraph of degree two with two components
(Figure 1(a)).
Theorem 1.1 (OpenAI [14, Theorem 1.1 and Corollary 7.1]). Let G be a finite simple graph that is
cubic, bipartite, planar and 3-connected, and let e be an edge of G. Then G has a Hamiltonian cycle that
does not contain e.
Here 3-connected means that G has at least four vertices and stays connected after deleting any two of
them. Barnette’s conjecture is the case without e. The edge e is there for the induction of Section 6,
which cuts G into smaller graphs and needs their cycles to agree on the cut. That the version with e is
equivalent to the conjecture goes back to Kelmans, as explained by Hertel [9, Corollary 3] and by Gorsky,
Steiner and Wiederrecht [8, Theorem 4.3].
The plan. The planar dual T has a vertex in each face of G and an edge across each edge of G. Each
vertex of G lies in a triangular face of T, coloured by its bipartition class (Figure 1(b)). A perfect
matching of G selects one side of every triangle. Its complement is connected exactly when the selected
sides contain no cycle: a cycle would separate the triangles inside it from those outside (Section 2). We
seek such an acyclic selection containing the side e0 that crosses e.
(1) Corner choices. Fix a black triangle t0 at e0. Removing e0 from the desired selection leaves three
trees, each containing one corner of t0. Direct them towards these corners. In each other black
triangle the selected side then points away from one corner, its tail, and every vertex off t0 is a
tail exactly once. Such a choice of corners is a state (Section 3).
(2) From a state back to a selection. The side we take must touch the chosen corner, so it must avoid
the opposite side. Call a state good when these opposite sides form three trees, each containing
one corner of t0 (Figure 1(c)). The sides that are not avoided then join the triangles into a tree,
and this tree forces a selection (panels (d)–(e)). A count called the disk identity proves that this
selection has no cycle.
(3) Two states. Another state, different in every triangle, orients the opposite sides with one edge
leaving every vertex off t0. This makes a state good as soon as its opposite sides contain no cycle
(Section 4).
(4) One count, two groupings. Give each pair a sign and a weight depending only on its second state.
A reversal pairs off pairs whose second state is unsuitable, with opposite signs and equal weights.
The arrows between the two chosen corners form cycles (Figure 1(f)). Reversing a clockwise cycle
flips the sign and raises the weight by the number of white triangles inside the cycle, which is at
least one. Grouped by these cycles, with the weight raised to a suitable power, the sum becomes
a sum of products of these numbers, all of one sign. So the sum is not zero, and a good state
survives.

History and sources. We follow Hertel’s survey [9] for the older history. Tait conjectured in 1884 that
cubic 3-connected planar graphs are Hamiltonian, and Tutte disproved this in 1946 with a non-bipartite
example [17]. Barnette asked whether bipartiteness rescues the statement. Before 2026 the conjecture
was known when all faces have four or six sides [9], under conditions on two of the three face colour
classes [5], and when all faces have at most eight sides [15]. Computer checks reached 64 vertices in work
of Holton, Manvel and McKay [9], and 90 vertices in work of Brinkmann, Goedgebeur and McKay [3]. In
a preprint dated 24 September 2026, OpenAI proved Theorem 1.1 [14]. The paired-state argument, disk
identity, flow argument and induction are theirs. States are the corner choices of Tutte’s theory of trinity,
as explained by Hine and Kálmán [10]. The target, two induced trees in T, is Stein’s reformulation [16]
in the form of Alt, Payne, Schmidt and Wood [2, Lemma 5]. Two expositions followed, one by Li [12],
who works in G, and one in an unsigned manuscript [4], which adds an exact criterion for the first step
and an enumeration algorithm. Remark 4.10 and Section 7 say how these accounts and ours differ.
The example. We follow one triangulation through every step (Figure 2). It has 13 vertices, 22 triangles
and no separating triangle, and its dual G has 22 vertices. It has 12 states and 8 pairs. All eight pairs

2. The dual triangulation and the target
The dual. Fix an embedding of G in the sphere, with edges drawn as polygonal arcs. Its dual T has a
vertex in each face of G and an edge crossing each edge of G once. Conversely G is the graph of faces of
T: each face of T contains one vertex of G, and two faces are adjacent in G when they share a side.
Lemma 2.1. Let G be as in Theorem 1.1. Then T is a simple graph with at least four vertices, every
face of T is bounded by a triangle, and the faces of T can be coloured black and white so that every edge
of T has one black and one white face.
Proof. First, G has no set of at most two edges whose removal separates a nonempty vertex set U from
the nonempty rest. If |U| = 1 then three edges leave U, and if |U| = 2 at least four do, since G is simple.
So |U| ≥3, and likewise for the rest. Deleting the at most two endpoints in U of the cut edges leaves a
nonempty part of U with no edge to the rest, contradicting 3-connectivity.
A loop of T, or two edges of T joining the same two vertices, is a closed curve that meets G in one
or two points, on one or two edges of G. The two ends of a crossed edge lie on opposite sides of the
curve, so both sides contain vertices of G, and the crossed edges form a cut of size at most two. Hence
T is simple. The face of T containing a vertex v of G is bounded by a closed walk through the three
faces of G at v, and in a simple graph a closed walk of length three is a triangle. Euler’s formula gives
|V (T)| = |F(G)| = 2 + |E(G)| −|V (G)| = 2 + |V (G)|/2 ≥4. Finally, colour the face of T containing v by
the class of v in the bipartition of G. The two faces at an edge of T contain the two ends of an edge of G,
so they get different colours.
□

From now on T is a coloured triangulation: a simple graph with at least four vertices, embedded in
the sphere so that every face is bounded by a triangle, with a black and white colouring of its faces in
which every edge has one face of each colour. Two faces share at most one side, since two faces with two
common sides would have the same three corners, and that triangle would bound both of them, leaving no
room for a fourth vertex. Euler’s formula needs a connected graph. The next lemma supplies connectivity
for T, for the inside of a cycle in Section 3 and for the pieces of Section 6.
Lemma 2.2. Let R be a finite graph embedded in the sphere such that every face of R is bounded by a
cycle of R. Then R is connected.
Proof. Let K be a component of R. The boundary of a face is a cycle, which is connected, so it lies in
one component. Let Ωbe the union of K and the faces whose boundary lies in K, and Ω′ the union of
the other components and the other faces. A point of K has a neighbourhood that meets only K and
faces with that point on their boundary, and these faces have their boundary in K. So Ωis open, and Ω′
is open for the same reason. They are disjoint, they cover the sphere, which is connected, and Ωis not
empty. Hence Ω′ is empty and R = K.
□
Each edge of T has exactly one black face and each black face has three sides, so the number of edges
is three times the number of black faces, and likewise for white faces. With Euler’s formula this gives
(2.3)
#{black faces} = #{white faces} = k,
|E(T)| = 3k,
|V (T)| = k + 2.
In the example k = 11 (Figure 2).
The target. A perfect matching of G is a set of edges of G meeting every vertex once. Read in T, it is a
set of edges of T containing exactly one side of every face.
Definition 2.4. A selection is a set P of edges of T that contains exactly one side of every face of T.
We write P ∗for the set of edges of G that cross the edges of P.
A selection matches each black face with the white face across its selected side, so it has k edges. The
question is which selections leave a connected graph in G. We need the answer for two kinds of edge set,
a selection here and a spanning tree in Section 3, so the next lemma is about an arbitrary set N of edges.
For a plane graph M and N ⊆E(M) write M ∗−N ∗for the spanning subgraph of the dual M ∗whose
edges cross the edges not in N.
Lemma 2.5 (duality). Let M be a connected plane graph and N ⊆E(M).
(1) If N contains a cycle Z, then an edge of M ∗joins a face inside Z to a face outside Z exactly
when it crosses an edge of Z, and M ∗−N ∗is disconnected.
(2) If N is acyclic, then M ∗−N ∗is connected. If N is a spanning tree of M, then M ∗−N ∗is a
spanning tree of M ∗.
Proof. (1) By the Jordan curve theorem Z splits the sphere into two connected open regions with boundary
Z, and every face of M lies in one of them. An edge of M ∗crosses only its own edge of M, so it joins
faces on opposite sides of Z exactly when it crosses an edge of Z. The two faces at an edge of Z lie on
opposite sides, so both sides contain faces, and every edge of M ∗between the two sides crosses an edge of
N and is missing from M ∗−N ∗.
(2) Suppose M ∗−N ∗is disconnected, and let Φ be the set of faces in one of its components. Call an
edge of M a boundary edge if one of its faces is in Φ and the other is not. A boundary edge lies in N,
since otherwise the edge of M ∗crossing it would leave Φ. Around a vertex v edges and faces alternate,
and an edge at v is a boundary edge exactly when the faces before and after it differ in membership of Φ.
Membership changes an even number of times around a circle, so every vertex meets an even number of
boundary edges. There is a boundary edge, for otherwise all faces at each vertex would agree, the two
ends of every edge would agree because they share the faces of that edge, and connectivity of M would
put all faces in Φ or none. A nonempty edge set with all degrees even contains a cycle, and this cycle
lies in N. If N is a spanning tree, then M ∗−N ∗is connected with |E(M)| −|V (M)| + 1 = |F(M)| −1
edges by Euler’s formula, so it is a spanning tree of M∗.
□
A reader who knows plane duality may prefer the classical proof of (2): contract a spanning tree
containing N to one vertex, which deletes the crossing edges from the dual and leaves the dual connected.
Proposition 2.6. Let P be an acyclic selection of a coloured triangulation T with dual G.
(1) The edges of G not in P ∗form a Hamiltonian cycle of G.
(2) P is a forest with exactly two components, and an edge of T lies in P exactly when its two ends
lie in the same component.
BARNETTE’S CONJECTURE
5
Proof. (1) Every face of T has one side in P, so every vertex of G meets one edge of P ∗, and since G is
cubic the other edges give every vertex degree two. By Lemma 2.5(2) with M = T and N = P they form
a connected graph, and a finite connected graph with all degrees two is a single cycle.
(2) P is acyclic with k edges on k + 2 vertices, so it has two components. Suppose an edge uv /∈P has
both ends in one component. Then P ∪{uv} contains a cycle Z through uv, and by Lemma 2.5(1) the
edges of G crossing Z form an edge cut of G. The Hamiltonian cycle of (1) meets this cut in exactly one
edge, the one crossing uv, because the other edges of Z are in P. But a cycle meets every edge cut in an
even number of edges.
□
Part (1) shows that the two conditions on the target do different jobs: one side per face gives degree
two, and acyclicity gives connectivity. Part (2) is the two-induced-trees form [16, 2], and we use it in
Lemma 3.1 and in the gluing. An acyclic selection containing an edge e0 of T gives a Hamiltonian cycle
of G that avoids the edge crossing e0, so Theorem 1.1 asks for an acyclic selection containing a prescribed
edge.
3. Corner choices and the tree of faces
Fix a face t0 of T and one of its sides e0 = ab, and let o be the third corner of t0. Exchanging the
colours if necessary, t0 is black; selections do not depend on the colours. We draw t0 as the outer face, so
that “inside” a cycle means on the side away from t0. The corners a, b, o are the roots. Let A be the set of
black faces other than t0 and X the set of vertices other than the roots. By (2.3), |A| = |X| = k −1 =: n.
Where the corner choices come from. Suppose P is an acyclic selection containing e0, and put
P0 = P \ {e0}.
Lemma 3.1. Each of the three components of P0 contains exactly one root. Orient every edge of P0
towards the root of its component, and for t ∈A let s(t) be the tail of the side of t in P0. Then s is a
bijection from A to X, and s(t) is a corner of t for every t.
Proof. By Proposition 2.6(2), a and b lie in one component of P and o in the other, because ao /∈P.
Deleting e0 splits the first component into a tree containing a and a tree containing b. In a tree oriented
towards its root every vertex other than the root has exactly one outgoing edge, so every vertex of X is
the tail of exactly one edge of P0, and the roots are tails of none. The side of t ∈A in P is not e0, which
lies in t0, so s(t) ∈X is defined. Distinct black faces have distinct selected sides, because an edge has
only one black face, and distinct edges of P0 have distinct tails, so s is injective; it is onto because every
x ∈X is the tail of an edge of P0, whose black face lies in A.
□
So the unknown is a choice of one corner in every face of A that uses every vertex of X once.
Definition 3.2. A state is a bijection s: A →X such that s(t) is a corner of t for every t ∈A.
We will build P from a state, and P will contain, in every t ∈A, one of the two sides of t at s(t). The
third side of t, opposite s(t), is excluded (Figure 3). Let Qs be the set of these opposite sides, one in
each face of A; they are distinct because an edge has only one black face, so |Qs| = n. In t0 the selection
must contain e0 and exclude ao and bo. Put Ss = Qs ∪{ao, bo}, the set of edges that every such selection
excludes; it has n + 2 = |V (T)| −1 elements.

The tree of faces. A selection that contains e0 and uses only sides at s(t) in each t ∈A is a selection
that avoids Ss. It pairs each face with the face across its selected side, and these two faces are adjacent
across an edge not in Ss. So consider the graph Ys = T ∗−S∗
s, whose nodes are the faces of T, two faces
being adjacent when they share a side not in Ss; it is a subgraph of G. A tree has at most one perfect
matching, found by matching a leaf to its neighbour, removing both and repeating. So if Ys is a tree, at
most one selection of this kind exists and no choice is left.
For Ys to be a tree we need the following condition on s. The condition is sufficient for what follows and
it is not necessary: the state that Lemma 3.1 reads off an acyclic selection need not satisfy it (Section 7).
Definition 3.4. A state s is good if Qs is a forest in which each component contains exactly one root.
The unsigned manuscript [4] calls a good state a tree matching.
Lemma 3.5. A state s is good if and only if Ss is a spanning tree of T.
Proof. Ss has |V (T)| −1 edges, so it is a spanning tree exactly when it is acyclic. That happens exactly
when Qs is acyclic and adding ao and bo closes no cycle, that is, when a, b and o lie in three different
components of Qs. A forest with n edges on n + 3 vertices has three components, so this means one root
in each.
□
Figure 5(a) shows the tree Ys and the selection of the next lemma for the state β of the example.
Lemma 3.6. Let s be a good state. Then Ys is a tree on the 2k faces of T, in which every face of A has
degree two and t0 has degree one. Root Ys at t0, and let Ps consist of the side that each black face shares
with its child. Then Ps is a selection, e0 ∈Ps, and for every t ∈A the side of t in Ps contains s(t).
BARNETTE’S CONJECTURE
7
Proof. Ys is a spanning tree of G by Lemmas 3.5 and 2.5(2). A face t ∈A has exactly one side in Ss, its
side in Qs, because ao and bo belong to t0. So t has degree two. The face t0 has ao, bo ∈Ss and e0 /∈Ss,
so it has degree one, and its neighbour is the white face y0 across e0. Colours alternate along every edge
of Ys. In the rooted tree, t0 has one child, every t ∈A has a parent and so exactly one child, and every
white face has a parent, which is black. Thus every black face has exactly one side in Ps. A white face y
is the only child of its parent, so the side towards its parent is in Ps. Any other side of y would be shared
with a black child t of y, and the side that t selects is shared with the child of t, which is not y; since two
faces share at most one side, that side is not in Ps. So every white face has exactly one side in Ps. The
side that t0 shares with y0 is e0, and for t ∈A the side shared with its child is not in Qs, so it is one of
the two sides at s(t).
□

For a good state Lemma 3.6 produces a selection Ps containing e0 without any further choice. It
remains to see that Ps has no cycle. A cycle in Ps \ {e0} would be made of sides leaving chosen corners,
and the rest of this section says what such a cycle looks like.
The inside of a cycle. Throughout the paper, the cycles we need are made of sides leaving corners
chosen by a state. Let r be a state, and suppose that in every face t ∈A one of the two sides at r(t) has
been chosen and directed out of r(t). We call these the chosen sides. The state is called r here because
Section 4 applies these facts to the first state of a pair.
Lemma 3.7 (outdegree). Let ⃗E be a set of edges of T, each directed, such that every vertex has at most
one outgoing edge in ⃗E. Then every cycle of ⃗E is a directed cycle. A component of ⃗E with ν vertices,
of which γ have no outgoing edge, has ν −γ edges. So γ ≤1, the component is a tree if γ = 1, and it
contains exactly one cycle if γ = 0.
Proof. A cycle with h edges has h distinct tails on its h vertices, so every vertex is the tail of one of its
edges. The edge count is the sum of the outdegrees, and a connected graph with ν vertices has at least
ν −1 edges, with equality for a tree, and exactly one cycle if it has ν.
□
The chosen sides have outdegree one at every vertex of X and zero at the roots, so Lemma 3.7 applies.
Let Z be a directed cycle of chosen sides, of length h. Every vertex of Z has an outgoing chosen side, so
it lies in X. The roots lie on the boundary of the outer face, and not on Z, so they lie outside Z. Hence

Euler’s formula needs a connected plane graph, so we first say what the inside of Z is. Let RZ consist of
Z and the vertices and edges of T inside Z. By the Jordan curve theorem the outside of Z is a connected
open region with boundary Z; it contains no point of RZ, so it is one face of RZ, bounded by the cycle
Z. Every other face of RZ lies inside Z and contains no vertex or edge of T, so it lies in one face of T;
conversely a face of T inside Z is a connected region disjoint from RZ whose boundary triangle lies in RZ.
So the faces of RZ are the B + W faces of T inside Z and the outside of Z, each bounded by a cycle, and
RZ is connected by Lemma 2.2. We also use that every face at a vertex strictly inside Z lies inside Z.
Lemma 3.8 (disk identity). Let r be a state and Z a directed cycle of chosen sides for r, of length h.
Let B and W be the numbers of black and white faces inside Z, and ℓthe number of edges of Z whose
black face is inside. Then W = B + 1 and h = 2ℓ+ 3. In particular h is odd and Z encloses at least one
white face.
Proof. Two counts hold for every cycle of T. The plane graph RZ has I + h vertices, B + W + 1 faces,
and (3(B + W) + h)/2 edges, since each inner face has three sides, an edge strictly inside lies on two inner
faces and an edge of Z on one; Euler’s formula gives the first count below. For the second, count each
side of an inner face with +1 if the face is black and −1 if it is white: an edge strictly inside contributes
+1 −1, and an edge of Z contributes +1 or −1 according to its inner face. Thus
B + W = 2I + h −2,
3(B −W) = 2ℓ−h.
The third count uses the state. Send each black face t inside Z to r(t), a vertex inside or on Z. This
is injective because r is. Every vertex v strictly inside is hit: v = r(t) for some t ∈A because r is onto
X, and t has the corner v, so it lies inside. A vertex v on Z is r(t) for exactly one t, and the edge of Z
leaving v is the chosen side of that t, because each face has only one chosen side and r is injective. So v
is hit exactly when that edge has its black face inside. This happens for ℓvertices of Z, so
B = I + ℓ.
Substituting into the first count gives W = I + h −ℓ−2, hence B −W = 2ℓ−h + 2, and the second
count becomes 3(2ℓ−h + 2) = 2ℓ−h, that is h = 2ℓ+ 3. Then W −B = h −2ℓ−2 = 1.
□

4. Pairs of states
We do not know how to point to a good state. This section shows that one exists, by a count in four
steps. A second corner choice turns goodness into the absence of cycles (Lemma 4.2). Every pair of
choices gets a sign, and the pairs that fail cancel in twos (Lemma 4.5). A weight, built from the white
faces that certain cycles enclose, lets the same sum be computed in a second way (Lemma 4.6). The
second computation shows that the sum is not zero (Proposition 4.8), so some pair does not fail.
Why two states. Goodness asks two things of Qs, no cycle and one root per component. The second
condition concerns whole components. Another state r that differs from s in every face reduces the second
condition to the first. It gives every vertex of X exactly one outgoing edge of Qs, and then a component
without a cycle contains exactly one root.

Lemma 4.2. Let (r, s) be a pair, and direct the edge of Qs in each t ∈A from r(t) to u(t). Then every
vertex of X has outdegree one and every root outdegree zero. Each component of Qs either is a tree
containing exactly one root, or contains no root and exactly one cycle, which is directed. So s is good if
and only if Qs is acyclic, and a good state has exactly one partner.
Proof. The edge of Qs in t joins r(t) and u(t), and r is a bijection onto X, which gives the outdegrees; the
rest of the first two sentences is Lemma 3.7. If s is good, a partner must direct each tree of Qs towards
its root, and r(t) is the tail of the edge of Qs in t. So r is determined. Conversely, directing the trees
towards their roots and taking tails defines a bijection r: A →X with r(t) ̸= s(t), because the edge of
Qs in t avoids s(t).
□
A pair determines a second set of edges, and it gives the second way of grouping the count. Let D(r, s)

directed as in Lemma 4.2. So the disk identity applies to every cycle of D(r, s) and to every cycle of Qs.

6. Separating triangles
Let ∆= xyz be a separating triangle of a coloured triangulation T, and let D be one of the two closed
disks it bounds. The piece TD consists of the vertices, edges and faces of T in D, together with one new
face, the cap, bounded by ∆on the other side.
BARNETTE’S CONJECTURE

Lemma 6.1. The three faces of T in D that have a side on ∆have the same colour. Colouring the cap
with the other colour makes TD a coloured triangulation with fewer vertices than T.
Proof. Count the sides of the faces of T in D with sign +1 for black and −1 for white. Edges inside D
cancel, so three times the number of black faces minus white faces in D is a sum of three terms ±1, one
for each side of ∆; being divisible by three, it is ±3, so the three terms agree. Every face of the piece is
bounded by a triangle, so the piece is connected by Lemma 2.2, and its graph is a subgraph of T, hence
simple. It has a vertex strictly inside D, so at least four vertices, and it misses the vertices strictly on the
other side. With the cap coloured oppositely, every side of ∆has faces of both colours, and the other
edges keep their two faces.
□

Theorem 6.2. Let T be a coloured triangulation, t0 a face of T and e0 a side of t0. Then T has an
acyclic selection containing e0.
Proof. We use induction on the number of vertices. If T has no separating triangle, exchange the colours
if necessary so that t0 is black. Then T has a pair by Proposition 5.2, a good state by Proposition 4.8,
and an acyclic selection containing e0 by Proposition 3.9.
Otherwise let ∆= xyz be a separating triangle, let D1 be the closed disk bounded by ∆that contains
t0 and D2 the other, and let T1, T2 be the pieces, coloured as in Lemma 6.1. The face t0 is a face of T1,
and by induction T1 has an acyclic selection P1 containing e0. The cap of T1 is bounded by ∆, so P1
contains exactly one side of ∆. Call it e′. The cap of T2 is also bounded by ∆, and by induction T2 has
an acyclic selection P2 containing e′, which is then its only side of ∆. Put P = P1 ∪P2.
P is a selection containing e0. Every face of T is a face of exactly one piece. Say f is a face of T1.
The edges that T1 and T2 share are the sides of ∆, and P2 contains only e′ among them, which is also in
P1. So f has the same sides in P as in P1, namely exactly one, and the same holds for faces of T2.
P is acyclic. By Proposition 2.6(2) applied in Ti, a side of ∆other than e′ has its ends in different
components of Pi. So if e′ = xy, then x and y lie in one component of Pi and z in the other, and the
only path in Pi between two of x, y, z is the edge e′. Suppose Z is a cycle in P. It is not contained in P1
or in P2, so it contains an edge of P2 \ P1, which is not a side of ∆and so has an end strictly inside D2.
Follow Z from this edge in both directions until it first meets {x, y, z}. The pieces meet only in x, y, z,
so this gives a path in P2 of length at least two between two vertices of {x, y, z}, and they are distinct
because Z is not contained in P2. This contradicts the previous paragraph.
□
The prescribed edge is what makes the gluing work: P2 must use the same side of ∆as P1, and an
arbitrary acyclic selection of T2 need not. Read in G, ∆is a cut of three edges, each piece is G with one
side of the cut contracted to a vertex, and the gluing joins two Hamiltonian cycles that use the same two

such cuts goes back to Kelmans; see [2, Section 5].

7. Remarks
How this account differs from the sources. The proof is that of [14], and its presentation here
differs in four places. The disk identity is stated as “one more white face than black”, Lemma 2.2 makes
Euler’s formula applicable to the inside of a cycle, and Proposition 3.9 reads the acyclicity of the selection
off that statement. The sign of a pair is real, as in [4], and is written as a product of local signs. The
weights are heights read along paths of faces. They are the weights that OpenAI construct in the proof
of [14, Lemma 5.3] for one choice of their circulations, and they are Li’s counts of crossings between
half-rays and matching edges [12, Section 4] taken along fixed paths. This choice removes the spokes and
the sliding argument of [14, Section 5.3], and the finite difference of Lemma 4.7 replaces the exponential
sum. The tree of faces Ys is obtained from the opposite sides by planar duality in T; in G it is Li’s black
dual trace [12, Section 6] with one extra leaf.
Which Hamiltonian cycles arise. For fixed t0 and e0, Lemma 3.1 assigns a state sC to every
Hamiltonian cycle C avoiding the edge across e0. C is produced by Proposition 3.9 exactly when sC
is good, and different good states give different cycles. If sC is good, the complement P of C avoids
SsC, because its side in each t ∈A contains sC(t) and its side in t0 is e0. Thus P and PsC are perfect
matchings of the tree YsC, and a tree has at most one perfect matching, so P = PsC. Conversely, when C
comes from a good state s, directing Ps \ {e0} out of s(t) gives outdegree one at each nonroot and zero at
each root. On each rooted tree this is its orientation towards the root, so Lemma 3.1 recovers sC = s.
This also proves that different good states give different cycles. In the example all six such cycles arise.
In the hexagonal prism, whose dual is the hexagonal bipyramid, take a black face as t0 and its side on
the equator as e0; there are three states, two of them good, and four Hamiltonian cycles avoiding the
edge, so only two arise. For the two other sides of t0 there are two such cycles, and both arise.
Why each hypothesis is needed. Bipartite. The colouring of the faces of T is the bipartition of G. It
gives every edge one black face, which makes Qs and D(r, s) consist of distinct edges and gives |A| = |X|.
Tutte’s 46-vertex graph [17] is cubic, planar and 3-connected but not Hamiltonian. The smallest such
graphs have 38 vertices [11].
Planar. On an orientable surface of genus g the same counting gives |V | = k +2−2g, so |X| = |A|−2g
and there are no states when g > 0. The smallest non-Hamiltonian cubic bipartite 3-connected graph is
the 50-vertex graph of Georges and Kelmans [7, 3].
Cubic. Cubicity makes the faces of T triangles, so that a corner has one opposite side, and it gives the
complement of a selection degree two. The incidence graph of the vertices and faces of the triangular
bipyramid has classes of sizes 5 and 6, so it has 11 vertices and no Hamiltonian cycle. It is planar, drawn
with each face centre joined to its three corners, and it is 3-connected. To check this, let the bipyramid
have equatorial vertices p1, p2, p3 and apices u, v, so that its faces are the six triangles upipj and vpipj,
and delete two vertices of the incidence graph.
• At most one of them is a face centre. The bipyramid stays connected when at most two of its five
vertices are deleted, as one sees from the equatorial triangle and the two apices. Each surviving
edge of the bipyramid lies on two faces and keeps the centre of at least one, so its ends are still
joined by a path of two edges. Each surviving face centre has a surviving corner.
• Both are face centres. Then all five vertices of the bipyramid survive. Two faces share at most
one side, so at most one edge of the bipyramid loses both of its face centres, and the bipyramid
minus one edge is connected. Each surviving face centre is joined to it.
In both cases the incidence graph stays connected.
3-connected. It is used once, to make T simple (Lemma 2.1). Simplicity is used in the density bound,
where a face of H of length two would break bal(Ψ) ≤dΨ −4, and in the pieces of Section 6. Take two
new vertices and three copies of the cube with one edge removed, and join the two ends of the removed
edge in each copy to the two new vertices, one to each, respecting the bipartition. The result is cubic,
bipartite and planar with 26 vertices. Deleting both new vertices leaves three components, so it has no
Hamiltonian cycle, because a cycle falls into at most two paths when two of its vertices are deleted. It is
BARNETTE’S CONJECTURE
19
2-connected all the same. Each cube with an edge removed is 2-connected and joins the two new vertices
by a path, so deleting one vertex leaves a connected graph:
• after deleting a new vertex, the three copies are joined through the other new vertex;
• after deleting a vertex of a copy, the rest of that copy is connected and joined to at least one new
vertex, and the other two copies still join the two new vertices.
Deciding Hamiltonicity is NP-complete for 2-connected cubic bipartite planar graphs [1].
No separating triangle. Proposition 5.2 uses it once, and it is not necessary: by [4, Theorem 1.2], a

No polynomial-time construction is known. The proof shows that a good state exists but gives
no efficient way to find one. The unsigned manuscript [4] states an algorithm that enumerates the good

no polynomial-time algorithm that finds a Hamiltonian cycle in every graph as in Theorem 1.1.
Consequences and open questions. By the equivalence of Gorsky, Steiner and Wiederrecht [8,
Theorem 4.16], Theorem 1.1 implies that every cubic, 3-connected, bipartite Pfaffian graph has a
Hamiltonian cycle through any given path of three edges [14, Corollary 7.2]. Kelmans showed that the
conjecture is equivalent to the statement that for any two distinct edges e, f on a common face there
is a Hamiltonian cycle through e that avoids f (as explained in [9, 2]), so that statement now holds
too. Whether the same holds for two arbitrary distinct edges e, f remains open. The argument above
prescribes only an avoided edge, and the gluing needs exactly that. The Pfaffian consequence uses a
universal equivalence: it passes from the planar theorem to cubic Pfaffian braces through trisums, then
to general cubic 3-connected bipartite Pfaffian graphs through tight-cut decompositions, as proved in [8,
Theorem 4.16].
OpenAI’s accompanying Lean formalisation gives a machine-checked proof of Barnette’s conjecture
[13]. It argues through algebraic duality rather than a drawing, does not check this exposition statement
by statement, and has no counterpart of Lemma 2.2 or of Proposition 2.6(2). On top of it, in its algebraic
model, Lemmas 4.4 and 4.7, the case of Lemma 4.5 that Proposition 4.8 uses, and Proposition 4.8 itself
have been checked in Lean by the argument given here, with the formalisation’s flow weights in place
of the heights of Section 4. With these in place of the complex phase and the polynomial of OpenAI’s
nonvanishing argument, their main theorem compiles unchanged. The Lean files accompany this paper in
the same repository, in the folder proofs/lean.
Two unpublished notes accompany this paper in the same repository. Barnette’s conjecture in the
cubic graph (proofs/primal/primal.pdf) gives the proof in the cubic graph G itself, lemma by lemma
and without the dual triangulation, with a dictionary between the two languages. Two involutions for the
good-pair lemma (proofs/involutions/involutions.pdf) gives the bijective proof by two involutions.
It writes out in full the argument that Li [12] intended for Proposition 4.8, with marked crossings in place
of the power ωm, and it is a term-by-term unpacking of Lemmas 4.5, 4.6 and 4.7 for one particular height.

Status: PROVED-HERE, a complete informal reconstruction, corrected after the inde-

The proof follows the checked Lean development at commit
4eaee87548250b2682affda7d05d947c05554bae, with two explicit departures: Li’s primal deficit
proof supplies the first pair, and real local signs replace Lean’s complex phases. STATUS.md

This note gives the proof of the project’s main paper (paper/main/barnette.pdf) in the
cubic graph G itself, lemma by lemma, with a dictionary at the end; two steps differ, since Li’s
deficit argument gives the first pair (Lemma 4) and flow potentials with a polynomial (Lemmas
6 and 8) replace the heights.
1. The target and the objects
Theorem T. Every finite simple cubic bipartite 3-edge-connected plane graph G has, for
every edge e0, a perfect matching P containing e0 such that G −P is connected. Consequently
every cubic bipartite 3-vertex-connected planar graph has a Hamiltonian cycle avoiding any
prescribed edge.
The connected complement of a perfect matching in a cubic graph has degree two at every
vertex, so it is one cycle. This is what we will construct. Working with 3-edge-connectivity keeps
the induction within precisely the hypotheses it needs.
Fix an orientation of the sphere, a bipartition B, W of V (G), and an edge e0 = b0w0 with
b0 ∈B. Write F for the faces of G. The three faces at b0 form R. Put
A = B \ {b0},
X = F \ R,
n = |A|.
We use faces as incidence labels. We never construct a triangulation, a spoke graph, or a
labelling by the two sides of the final Hamiltonian cycle. A face link is simply an edge e of G,
regarded as joining its two incident faces. A face circuit is a cyclic list of distinct faces f0, . . . , fh−1
and distinct edges ei with ei incident with fi, fi+1, with indices modulo h. This is an incidence
description on G; no drawn arcs through faces are required. Forest and connected-component
language for face links means the corresponding ordinary finite incidence relation on the face
labels. Face circuits are precisely cycles of the dual graph G∗. This relation retains the cycle-cut
content of planar duality. Avoiding the triangulation does not remove that content.
2. The planar facts, with their scope stated
A plane graph here is a finite oriented combinatorial map of genus zero, not a geometric
drawing. Its darts have an edge-reversing involution and a cyclic successor at each vertex.
Following a dart and the prescribed successor at its end traces a facial boundary. Isolated
vertices are retained when taking subgraphs. For disconnected subgraphs, a face can have
several boundary walks; its boundary components are grouped by the inherited map. All planar
operations below are finite operations on these lists.
The sole imported planar theorem is Euler’s formula, v −e+f = 1+c for a sphere map with c
connected components. We use the following elementary map rules. Reversing a dart reverses its
contribution, so coherently oriented facial boundaries give opposite coefficients on the two sides of
every edge. Deleting an edge with distinct incident faces splices their boundary lists and merges
those faces. An edge with the same face on both sides is a bridge in genus zero: otherwise its
deletion keeps its component connected and splits its boundary list, contradicting Euler. Deleting
Date: 14 November 2026, refereed revision.
1
2
BARNETTE’S CONJECTURE IN THE CUBIC GRAPH
that bridge splits the component and its boundary walk, but leaves the face count unchanged.
Deleting an isolated vertex also leaves the face count unchanged. Contracting a nonloop edge
splices its two vertex rotations and preserves the facial regions and genus. These assertions
follow by removing the two darts and checking their successors, with Euler distinguishing the
bridge case.
A subgraph inherits its embedding by these deletions. Each surviving facial boundary bounds
a face containing the original face on that side; a deleted vertex occupies one of the resulting
faces. In particular each face of a family whose entire boundary survives is still a face, and
an omitted vertex lies in another face. This is the subgraph rule used in Lemma 4. The
boundary-walk cut-vertex criterion used in Lemma 1 follows by splitting a repeated vertex into
its two intervening rotation intervals: splitting the two occurrences splits that facial boundary
as well, increasing both the vertex count and the number of facial boundary walks by one while
leaving the edges fixed. Apply Euler separately to the resulting rotation components, where
the sum of vertex counts minus edge counts plus facial-walk counts is twice the number of
components. It increases by two, so there is one extra component. The two new boundary walks
belong to the same global face; the global face count does not increase. The two rotation intervals
cannot be joined away from the original vertex. Thus a 2-connected sphere map has cyclic
facial boundaries. These rules specify the finite planar background used below; no geometric
separation or isotopy theorem is imported.
General circuit-cut fact. PROVED-HERE. In a connected sphere map, face circuits are
exactly bonds, and each bond has connected shores. This assertion allows loops and parallel
face links.
Proof. We give the cycle-cut argument without drawing a separating curve. Over F2, the
boundary vectors of the faces span the cycle space of G. Here is the standard Euler proof of this
fact. Their sum is zero. Every other dependence assigns equal coefficients to the two faces at
each edge. All faces are linked by successive edge incidences, so those coefficients are all equal.
Face-incidence connectivity follows, for example, by contracting a spanning tree and deleting
the remaining loops one by one. The resulting one-vertex graph remains connected at each
deletion, so Euler forces its face count to fall by one; that deletion merges its two incident faces.
Eventually only one face remains. Thus the boundary span has dimension |F|−1 = |E|−|V |+1,
the cycle-space dimension. Facial boundaries are even-degree edge sets, so their span is the
whole cycle space.
An edge set is therefore a cut exactly when it meets every facial boundary evenly. For
completeness, the orthogonal complement of the cycle space is the cut space: if an edge indicator
has even sum on every cycle, its path sum from a fixed vertex is independent of the path; its
value on an edge is the difference of the two vertex path sums. In characteristic two this is the
cut of the vertices assigned value one.
A face circuit meets each of its faces twice, and all other faces zero times, so is a cut. A
proper nonempty subset cannot meet all those faces evenly: following the cyclic list propagates
the choice of one edge to all of them. Hence this cut is a bond. Conversely, the edge set of a cut
gives an even-degree face-link relation. A nonempty such relation contains a circuit, which is
itself a cut by the argument just given. Minimality of a bond makes it that single circuit. The
assertions include loops or parallel face links if present; 3-edge-connectivity rules out circuits of
length one or two.
A cut is minimal precisely when both shores are connected. If a shore had two components, the
boundary of one would be a proper nonempty subcut. Conversely, if both shores are connected,

Proof of Theorem T. Apply strong induction on |V (G)|, with the quantifier "for every edge
e0" retained. If there is no nontrivial three-edge cut, Lemmas 4 through 12 prove the assertion.
Otherwise use Lemma 13. Choose as the first cap a side on which e0 remains an edge; if e0

omits exactly one cap edge, say a. In the other cap use induction with prescribed avoided edge
a. The cycles glue by Lemma 13. If e0 is internal to the first side, its avoidance persists. If it is
a boundary edge, it is precisely a and is again avoided. The complement is the desired matching
containing e0.
Finally a cubic 3-vertex-connected graph is 3-edge-connected in the present setting. To see
this directly, suppose a cut had at most two edges. Each shore has at least three vertices: a
singleton has three outgoing edges, and a two-vertex set has at least four in a simple cubic graph.
Delete the at most two cut endpoints on one shore. A vertex remains on that shore and all
vertices remain on the other, with no path between them. This contradicts 3-vertex-connectivity.
A planar graph drawn on the sphere has a genus-zero rotation system, read off from the cyclic
order of edges at each vertex; this standard translation is the one place where drawings, and so
the Jordan curve theorem, enter. The theorem therefore applies to every graph in Barnette’s
conjecture.
9. What each hypothesis does
Finiteness supplies the enumerations, minima, flow network, and strong induction. Simplicity
is automatic once |V | > 2: bipartiteness excludes loops, and parallel edges at u, v leave at most
two edges leaving {u, v}, contradicting 3-edge-connectivity unless these are all vertices. We keep
the word because Barnette’s conjecture is stated for simple graphs. Cubicity supplies three
incident faces, the unique opposite edge, the four counts, the recovery-tree degrees, and the
cap degrees. Bipartiteness supplies balanced incidence parts, the local black-edge labels, the
colour counts, and the matching recovery. Planarity supplies Lemmas 1 through 3 and Euler in
Lemma 4, and survives capping. Three-edge-connectivity makes G 2-connected, giving facial
cycles and three distinct faces at each vertex in Lemma 1. It makes face links simple, survives
capping as the induction hypothesis, and gives connected shores and three distinct ends for
nontrivial three-edge cuts in Lemma 13. Lemma 4 obtains c ≥3 from positive divisibility, not
from 3-edge-connectivity. The additional absence of nontrivial three-edge cuts is used only in
Lemma 4.

face is used once, the tail is incident with b and differs from s(b), so this defines a partner. The
orientation toward a root is forced, proving uniqueness. There are three components since Qs has
n edges and n + 3 vertices. Lemma 9 adds two root-face links. These join the three components
into a face tree exactly when the three roots lie in distinct components. Indeed, all added edges
have root endpoints, so a rootless component cannot be joined. By the circuit-cut test and the
edge count, that face tree condition is equivalent to its complementary primal graph being a
tree. This proves every assertion.
Remark 15, compatible matchings. PROVED-HERE. For a fixed black root and a perfect
matching P, there exists a compatible state exactly when G −P is connected. The compatible
state is unique.
Proof. The forward direction is Lemma 12. Conversely suppose the complement C is connected.
The face links in P have no circuit, since such a circuit would be a cut disjoint from C. They
form a forest with two components, since |P| = n + 1 and there are n + 3 faces. Let e0 be the
matching edge at the root; it joins two root faces. Each of the other two root edges has its ends in
different components of this forest. Otherwise the path between its faces in P, together with that
edge, would be a face circuit and hence a cut met by the cycle C exactly once, impossible since
every cycle meets every cut evenly. The third root face therefore lies in the other component
from the two ends of e0. Removing e0 leaves three trees, one per root. Orient these toward their
roots and assign to each b ∈A the tail face of its matching edge. This gives a bijection onto X
and a face incident with the matching edge, hence the required state. Every compatible state
must give this same orientation, proving uniqueness.
COMPUTED before these proofs: the independent referee checked 25,272 forest-state/root-
edge cases without a partner, 3,256 forest states with a partner, and 186,476 matching/root pairs
on 56 graph records with 8 to 24 primal vertices. The records include the cube twice. The three
observations held throughout that range. See the referee’s code/README.md for commands.
These finite observations motivated Remarks 14 and 15; they do not replace the proofs. The tree-
matching criterion in research/2026-11-14_sol_referee-structure/INTEGRATION.md, Sections
5 and 7, describes the same one-root-per-component condition through the incidence graph.
Remark 15 covers every Hamiltonian complement, but does not assert that every compatible
state is itself a forest state with a partner.

TWO INVOLUTIONS FOR THE GOOD-PAIR LEMMA
Abstract. We write out the intended multi-mark proof in Appendix B of Zhentao Li’s note.
The proof uses finite signed sets and two explicit involutions. It uses no generating function,
limiting argument, or complex number. A finite alternating path constructs a good pair. The
coefficient comparison at the end is a separate verification, not a premise of the proof.
1. Contract and notation
Let T be a finite simple sphere triangulation whose faces have a proper black and white
colouring. Put a black face t0 outside, and let R be its three corners. Write A for the other
black faces and X = V (T)\R. Counting sides gives equally many black and white faces. Euler’s
formula then gives |A| = |X| = n. A state is a bijection s : A →X selecting a corner of each
face. A pair p = (r, s) is an ordered pair of states with r(t) ̸= s(t) everywhere. Let Qs have the
side opposite s(t) in every t ∈A and all vertices of T.
Theorem 1 (Good-pair lemma). If a pair exists, a pair exists for which Qs is a forest.
We call a pair (r, s) for which Qs is a forest a good pair. Earlier versions of this note said
forest pair. Its second state is a good state in the sense of the main paper, by Lemma 4.2 there.
This note accompanies the project’s main paper, The proof of Barnette’s conjecture: an
exposition, in the same repository. Through that Lemma 4.2, Theorem 1 is its Proposition 4.8.
The proof here is Li’s intended proof written out in full, and in the form of Section 5 it is a
term-by-term unpacking of the main paper’s Lemmas 4.5 to 4.7 for one particular height.
This is OpenAI Proposition 5.1.
It is the cancellation part of Li’s Key Lemma 7.
Li’s
preliminary existence of a pair requires additional graph hypotheses; Theorem 1 does not.
Throughout the proof we assume a pair exists. We do not assume that T has no separating
triangle. In Li’s incidence language delete the outer black centre and its three root corners,
obtaining the balanced incidence graph on A and X. The union of the two states is a 2-factor
there. After deleting the second matching, each remaining black centre joins the two corners of
its opposite side, with root endpoints removed. A cycle is therefore exactly a subdivided cycle
of Qs avoiding roots. Every cycle of a partnered Qs avoids roots by the outdegree argument in
Lemma 4 below. Consequently the forest conclusion is exactly Li’s cycle-breaking condition.
Place a centre in each bounded black face and join it to its corners by spokes.
A plane
straight-line drawing exists, and a small rotation makes every vertical line through a white-face
point miss all vertices and centres. Choose a point w in each white face, also in this general
position.
Write ρw for the upward ray starting at w.
All its intersections with spokes are
transverse and in their interiors. This choice is fixed once. The proof also works with fixed
simple paths to infinity, provided each individual crossing is retained as a separate token.
2. The disk count and the sign
For an oriented edge u →v of T, put δ(u, v) = 1 when its black face lies to its left, and −1
otherwise.
Lemma 2 (Disk identity). Select one outgoing side from the corner chosen by a state in every
face of A. A simple directed cycle among these sides encloses no root. If it has length h and
ℓof its boundary sides have their black face inside, then h −2ℓ= 3. Its length is odd, its disk
contains a white face, and its δ-sum is −3 counterclockwise and 3 clockwise.
Proof. Roots lie on the outside triangle and no selected side has a root as tail. Thus the cycle
avoids roots and its bounded disk contains none. Let I count strictly interior vertices and B, W
the black and white faces inside the disk. State bijectivity gives B = I + ℓ. Indeed the state is

injective, and an inside triangle selects a vertex of the closed disk. An interior vertex is selected
by some triangle, which contains it and so lies inside. A boundary vertex is selected by the
triangle supplying its outgoing boundary side, which lies inside exactly for the ℓspecified sides.
So the inside triangles correspond to the I interior vertices and those ℓboundary vertices. If E
counts disk edges, side counting gives
E = 3B + h −ℓ= 3W + ℓ.
The closed disk with its triangulation is connected: its underlying space is a disk, and its
triangles join along their edges and vertices. Its faces are exactly the triangles counted above.
Euler’s disk formula is I + h −E + B + W = 1. Substitute B = I + ℓand the first edge count
to get W = B + 1. Equating edge counts now gives h −2ℓ= 3. The asserted signs follow by
traversing the disk boundary. In particular W ≥1.
□
Direct the side in t from r(t) to s(t). These sides form a directed cycle cover Dp of X. There
are no repeated undirected edges, since each edge has exactly one black face. As in the main
paper, the undirected edge set of Dp is the cover of p. The cycles are simple, have odd length,
and enclose a white face by Lemma 2. Define

It is the number of clockwise cycles minus the number of counterclockwise cycles. If c(p) counts
cycles then J(p) ≡c(p) ≡n (mod 2). Let m = minp c(p). Thus m ≥1. This is the m of the
main paper, and a cover with m cycles is a minimum cover.
Replace every directed side r(t) →s(t) by the two-spoke route r(t) →t →s(t). Its cycles
have the same orientation and enclose the same white-face points. Indeed, each detour lies in
the interior of its own black triangle apart from its two ends, and distinct triangles have disjoint
interiors, so the route is a simple closed polygon. It differs from the side cycle by the boundaries
of the small triangles r(t), t, s(t), which contain no white-face point. Winding numbers at white-
face points are therefore equal. Lemma 2 puts a white-face point inside, where both winding
numbers are ±1, so the orientations agree. We call these the spoke cycles of p.
Definition 3. A token is a crossing (w, t) of ρw with the spoke t →s(t). An object is o = (p, M),
where M is an unordered set of exactly m distinct tokens. The same white face may occur more
than once, with different spokes. The same spoke may occur more than once, with different
white faces. The identical crossing may not occur twice. Let Ωbe this finite set. It depends on
the drawing, since a ray swept past a vertex or a centre gains or loses crossings. Only its signed
size is used, and Lemma 6 shows that the signed size does not depend on the drawing. For a
token let d(w, t) = 0 if the spoke t →s(t) goes left to right across the ray and 1 otherwise. Give
the object sign
σ(o) = (−1)⌊J(p)/2⌋+P
(w,t)∈M d(w,t).
This is the set convention in Li’s Definition 14. Li orients his incidence cycles oppositely to
our two-spoke routes: his cw′ = −J and each of his crossing directions is the opposite of ours.
These changes multiply our sign by (−1)n+m = 1. Our sign therefore agrees with Li’s. An
ordered list convention also works, including repeated tokens. Its fixed objects are m! labelled
versions of ours. We use sets to avoid that extra multiplicity.
3. First involution: keep the second state
Fix total orders on unoriented simple cycles. Both maps compare only cycles of one Qs or of
one Dp, which use disjoint sets of faces, so the lexicographic order on sorted supplying-face sets
suffices. Cycle choices below never use their current direction. If Qs is a forest, define ι1(o) = o.
Otherwise choose its first cycle K using s alone. Write u(t) for the third corner of t. On faces
supplying K, replace r(t) by u(t); retain s and all tokens.
Lemma 4. The map ι1 is an involution. Its fixed objects are exactly those with Qs a forest,
and it reverses sign at every other object.

Proof. Orient every side of Qs from r(t) to u(t). Every nonroot has outdegree one and every
root has outdegree zero. On a simple cycle, its h edges have distinct tails among its h vertices.
Hence each vertex is a tail exactly once, and the cycle is directed. Reversing it permutes the
selected vertices cyclically and preserves the bijection r. The third corner is never s(t), so the
resulting states remain disjoint. Since s is fixed, tokens stay valid and the same cycle is selected
again. Reversing twice restores r. For each changed triangle the cyclic orders give
δ(u(t), s(t)) −δ(r(t), s(t)) = 2δ(r(t), u(t)).
Lemma 2 on K changes J by 2 or −2. Its floor half changes by an odd integer, while all crossing
directions stay fixed. This proves sign reversal. A nonempty cycle changes r, so it creates no
fixed object.
□
4. Second involution: pair successive crossings
For an unoriented spoke cycle C, list its crossings with ρw starting at w, with indices 1, . . . , k.
If w is outside C, k is even; pair indices 1 ↔2, 3 ↔4, . . .. If w is inside, k is odd; leave index
1 unpaired and pair 2 ↔3, 4 ↔5, . . ..
Call this partial pairing PC,w.
It depends only on
the drawing, C, and w. When C is directed it is traversed r(t) →t →s(t), so an s-spoke is
traversed away from its centre and an r-spoke towards it; after reversal of C the old r-spoke
is an s-spoke traversed away from the centre. Two paired crossings have opposite directions of
traversal, because consecutive crossings alternate entry and exit.
Here is ι2 on o = (p, M), in priority order.
(1) If a spoke cycle carries no token, reverse the first such cycle, exchanging r and s on it;
retain M.
(2) Otherwise every cycle carries a token. There are at least m cycles and exactly m tokens.
Consequently there are exactly m cycles and one token on each. Write that token on
C as (wC, tC). Choose the first cycle for which wC is outside C, if any. If none exists,
choose the first cycle whose token is not crossing number 1. If neither exists, fix the
object.
(3) On the chosen cycle, move its sole token to its partner under PC,wC. If the partner spoke
currently belongs to s, retain the pair. If it belongs to r, reverse that cycle, then retain
the moved token as an s-token. Leave the other tokens unchanged.
Lemma 5. This defines an involution on Ωwhich reverses sign off its fixed set. Its fixed objects
have exactly m cycles, one token on each, whose white-face point is inside that cycle and whose
crossing is first along its ray.
Proof. Cycle reversal exchanges two perfect matchings on an alternating cycle, so it preserves
valid pairs and the underlying unoriented cycles. In case 1 the reversed cycle carries no token, so
every token keeps its spoke as an s-spoke and M is a token set of the new pair. The same cycles
remain unmarked. The same first cycle is chosen twice, and no token changes membership or
direction. Reversal changes J by 2 or −2, so the sign reverses.
In case 2 exactly one token is assigned to each cycle. The partner exists because the sole
unpaired crossing is excluded by the selection rule. If its spoke is an r-spoke, reversal makes it
an s-spoke. No other token on that cycle can become invalid, because there is no other token
there. Tokens on distinct cycles have distinct spokes, so the moved token cannot collide with
another token. Its white point and assigned cycle stay the same.
Thus the first selection test, exterior white point, is invariant. If that test selects no cycle,
the second test, nonfirst crossing, is invariant: the paired indices are both different from 1.
All earlier cycles keep their status. The same first cycle is therefore selected on the second
application. The geometric crossing pairing reverses itself. If no reversal was made, its old
spoke is still an s-spoke, so the return move makes no reversal. If a reversal was made, the old
spoke is now an r-spoke, so the return move reverses the same cycle again. In both cases the
original object returns.
If no reversal is made, J is unchanged and the direction of the moved token flips, because
paired crossings have opposite directed crossings. If reversal is made, the geometric pairing and

the cycle reversal each flip that direction, so its final direction is unchanged; meanwhile ⌊J/2⌋
changes parity. Other tokens lie on other cycles and keep their directions. Both cases reverse
sign. Every nonfixed rule changes the pair or token, which also proves the asserted fixed-set
description.
□
Lemma 6. The fixed set of ι2 is nonempty and every member has sign (−1)⌊m/2⌋. In fact its
cardinality is

Proof. For any minimum cover choose a white face inside each cycle, possible by Lemma 2.
Different cycles may choose the same white face. The first crossing of its ray with its spoke
cycle exists. Orient each cycle so that this spoke belongs to s. The two orientations exchange the
spoke labels, so exactly one orientation works. The choices on distinct cycles are independent.
The resulting tokens are distinct, even for repeated white faces, since their spokes are on distinct
cycles. They give a fixed object. Conversely the fixed-set description recovers these choices
uniquely, which proves the cardinality formula.
If q cycles are counterclockwise, their first exits cross right to left, and clockwise first exits
cross left to right.
Thus the direction sum is q and J = m −2q.

Proof of Theorem 1. Partition Ωinto positive and negative objects. If ι1 had no fixed point it
would biject these two sets. But ι2 pairs opposite signs except for its nonempty fixed set of one
sign. The two cardinalities therefore differ by (−1)⌊m/2⌋F ̸= 0. A fixed object of ι1 exists, and
its underlying pair has Qs a forest.
□
5. Marks without a drawing
The following version uses only the oriented sphere map, its face incidences, and a fixed
tree in the dual graph rooted at t0. No coordinates, rays, or general-position choices enter
its definitions. A side of a simple cycle is inside when it does not contain t0, and the cycle
is counterclockwise when its inside lies to its left; with this reading Lemma 2 and J need no
drawing. For each white face w let w = f0, f1, . . . , fj = t0 be its tree path. Its faces are distinct,
and only the last is t0. At each black face t = fi with 0 < i < j, the entering and leaving
sides meet in a corner v. Set κw(i) = 1 if this turn has v on its left and −1 if it has v on its
right, using the orientation of the sphere map. This is the turn convention of the main paper,
Section 4. A token for s is the incidence (w, i) with fi ∈A and s(fi) = v. Its direction bit is
d(w, i) = (1 + κw(i))/2. Keep exactly m distinct tokens and the same sign formula as before.
Since a tree path visits a face at most once, (w, i) also determines its black face; retaining the
step makes the definition explicit.
For a spoke cycle C, its list at w consists of the steps turning around either r(t) or s(t) for
t on C, in increasing path order. A spoke here means the formal incidence of a triangle with a
corner. Such incidences have their cyclic order from the sphere map.
Lemma 7. Let C be a spoke cycle of a pair and w a white face.
(1) The list of C at w has odd length exactly when w is inside C.
(2) At consecutive entries of the list, C crosses the path in opposite directions.
(3) If w is inside C, then at the first entry C crosses the path from right to left when C is
counterclockwise, and from left to right when it is clockwise.
Consequently Lemmas 4, 5, 6 and 8 and the proof of Theorem 1 hold for path tokens, with these
lists in place of the ray lists and with the same number F.
Proof. Subdivide every black triangle of A into three sectors by its formal centre-to-corner
incidences. Each sector contains one side of the triangle, and the sectors on two sides share
the incidence at their common corner. A step that enters t by one side and leaves by another
therefore passes from one sector to the next. It crosses the incidence at their common corner
TWO INVOLUTIONS FOR THE GOOD-PAIR LEMMA
5
v once and neither of the other two. If v is on the left of the step, the incidence directed away
from the centre points to the left, so it crosses the path from right to left. With left to right
counted positive, its signed crossing is −κw(i). Reversing the incidence changes this sign. This
is a check of the two cyclic orders of the entering and leaving sides, so it uses no lengths or
angles.
The incidence cycle C is simple, since its corners and its centres are distinct.
Cut the
subdivided sphere map along it. The two components are its inside disk and its outside disk.
They contain the same white faces as the two sides of the side cycle, because the two cycles differ
only by the sectors on the sides r(t)s(t). The refined face path changes components exactly
when it crosses an incidence of C. In a triangle t on C these are the incidences at r(t) and s(t),
crossed by the turns around r(t) and s(t); a turn around u(t) crosses neither. In white faces, in
t0 and in triangles off C the path crosses no incidence of C. So the path changes components
exactly at the listed steps, and successive listed steps alternate exit and entry. The path ends in
t0 on the outside, so its list is odd exactly when w is inside. At a first exit, a counterclockwise
cycle traverses the incidence from right to left relative to the path, and a clockwise cycle from
left to right. These statements can also be read directly from the oriented boundary of the inside
disk. If the incidence is an s-incidence its traversal is away from the centre; an r-incidence is
traversed towards it. Thus the direction bit above has exactly the convention of Definition 3.
The first map retains s, so it retains token eligibility and every bit. In the second map an
unmarked cycle can still be reversed without changing any token. Otherwise minimality again
forces one token on each of m cycles. Pair consecutive list entries with the same index rules
as before. The common white face, the unoriented cycle, and the status of an entry as first or
nonfirst are unchanged by this pairing and any cycle reversal. The partner lies on r or s exactly
as before; reversal when it lies on r makes it eligible. Distinct cycles have distinct incidences,
so no other token is lost or duplicated. The return move makes the same reversal decision.
Alternating traversal signs give the same two sign-reversal cases in Lemma 5.
For each enclosed white face the odd list has a first entry. Exactly one orientation of its cycle
makes this an s-incidence. Independent choices on distinct cycles give exactly the same product
F. If q cycles are counterclockwise, the first-exit rule gives direction sum q and J = m −2q,
so every fixed sign is (−1)⌊m/2⌋. The counting proof and the finite alternating-path proof now
apply without any further change.
□
The tree is a convenience. The proof uses only that each path is simple and ends at t0, so
any fixed family of such paths serves, as in the main paper. The marked-set size, first-fixed
count, and path lengths depend on the chosen paths, even though they require no drawing. The
minimum m, the enclosed-face counts, F, the common fixed sign and the signed sum depend
only on the rooted oriented triangulation. The identities of fixed marked objects depend on the
paths; their number does not. Let H(s) be the signed number of tokens of s, a token counting
+1 when κw(i) = −1 and −1 when κw(i) = 1; Section 8 defines the same quantity for rays. For
this version H(s) = −P
w ηs(w) = −ω(s) exactly, with the main paper’s turn heights for the
same paths and the same orientation of the sphere. So H has the opposite sign to the main
paper’s weight ω. For rays the same cycle-reversal increments hold; an additive constant may
differ between covers. This is a term-by-term bijective unpacking of the height proof for this
particular height. The first involution is its cancellation lemma on marked objects. The second
proves its height and finite-difference lemmas together by pairing the terms of the expansion.
The number of marks matters. With fewer than m marks every object has an unmarked
cycle, so the signed count is zero. With more than m, the one-token-per-cycle deduction fails
and the second map is undefined on some objects. COMPUTED in the referee’s ray drawings:
with m −1 marks the count is zero on all 880 paired roots through 14 vertices; with m + 1 it
is zero on 57 of them, versus 78 in the original author’s drawings. These higher-order counts
depend on the rays. Thus arbitrary mark counts cannot replace m.
6
TWO INVOLUTIONS FOR THE GOOD-PAIR LEMMA
6. An explicit constructor
Enumerate pairs to determine m and a minimum cover. Choose its white faces and orient
its first crossings as in Lemma 6, obtaining an ι2-fixed object. Apply ι1; if it fixes the object,
return the pair. Otherwise apply ι2, then ι1, and continue, stopping before a fixed move.
Lemma 8. This procedure terminates at a good pair without repeating an object.
Proof. Put an undirected edge of label i between distinct objects exchanged by ιi.
Retain
parallel edges if the two maps have the same image. Each vertex has at most one edge of either
label. The starting point has no edge of label 2. Its component is therefore a finite alternating
path or a single vertex; a degree-one vertex cannot lie on a cycle, including a two-edge parallel
cycle. Traversal never repeats a vertex. If the other endpoint also lacked label 2, the path would
start and end with label 1 and have odd length. Every edge reverses sign. The endpoint would
therefore be an ι2-fixed object of opposite sign, contrary to Lemma 6. The other endpoint must
lack label 1 and yields a forest. An isolated starting object already has that property.
□
This is the finite path argument of the Garsia–Milne involution principle, proved here rather
than invoked as a black box.
It requires a minimum cover at initialization.
The marked
construction in A constructive proof, Section 5.1, starts at an arbitrary pair, uses ordered weight
tokens and may restart with fewer cycles. We make no efficiency claim for our minimum search.
A bound on the subsequent path is |Ω| −1 moves.

Li’s Definitions 13–23 and Lemmas 34–35 give exactly the one-token version.
Claim 25
is the disk count and Lemma 17 is our first sign change.
Definition 14 states the set con-
vention.
Appendix B states the rule for an unmarked cycle, the case of exactly cmin cy-
cles with one mark each, the priority rule (using the total order on cycles fixed in Li’s Sec-
tion 4.3), the reversal along a single cycle in the exterior case, the fixed set and its sign.
It does not prove that all-marked objects have one mark per cycle, that the map is an in-
volution, or that it reverses sign; it says only “switch to the other edge” in the interior
nonfirst case, where the cycle must also be reversed when the partner belongs to the other
matching; and it does not show that the fixed set is nonempty, which needs an indepen-
dent orientation choice on each minimum cycle. The project’s dependency audit of Li’s note
(research/2026-11-14 fable dependency-graph/audit-li.md, items L-F5 and L-F6) first
identified these steps and sketched them. Lemmas 5 and 6 write them out for every m.
These cases occur early. At m = 2 a set of two tokens can lie entirely on one cycle, so Li’s
unmarked-cycle rule is used. At m = 3 a reversal on a singly marked cycle must leave the other
two token directions intact, as Li’s M1△Ci does; the global interchange (M2, M1) of Li’s one-
cycle case would not. Concrete pairs and their images are recorded in witnesses.json. They
use the 9-vertex class 0 root 0 and the 12-vertex class 0 root 0, respectively, in the canonical
census encoding. Their marked sets have 40 and 1200 objects and their second fixed sets have
4 and 28 objects. The first separator-free example in this census with m = 3 is the 14-vertex
class 27, root 0. It has 826 marked objects and eight second-fixed objects. Its full face list and
a nonfixed move are recorded in nonseparating-witness.json. Thus the multi-mark checks
cannot be bypassed by restricting to triangulations without separating triangles. The interior
nonfirst-crossing branch occurs already at m = 2 on 11-vertex class 1, root 0. Its exact object
and image appear in polynomial-comparison.json.
Li also invokes the bipartite 2-factor criterion without explicitly counting the two sides. For
a cubic bipartite plane graph on N vertices, Euler gives N/2+2 faces. Removing the root black
vertex and its three incident faces leaves N/2 −1 vertices on each incidence side. This supplies
the required balance condition. Our theorem assumes a pair and does not use that criterion.

An atlas of proof routes for Barnette's conjecture
Readings of one proof, each drawn on a computed example. The proof is the one in the OpenAI paper:
every cubic, bipartite, 3-connected planar graph G has a Hamiltonian cycle. Most pages use one trian-
gulation T with 13 vertices, the dual of a graph G with 22 vertices. Black faces of T are grey, the outer
black face is the grey collar, and the three roots are hollow. A state is a set of filled corner wedges, one
in each black face. Page 1 is the map. The last page lists where each picture and number comes from.

(a) The state s1. It is good: its opposite edges
(dashed) form three trees, one hanging from each root.
(b) Delete the chosen spoke in each black face
(dotted). The other spokes form a spanning tree
(bold), so the curves crossing the deleted spokes form
a tree on the white faces. The ringed white face
touches e.
(c) Each tree edge passes two sides of its black face.
Select the side nearer the leaves, and add e: 11
selected edges, one on every face.
(d) The selected edges are two trees (disks, squares)
through all 13 vertices, with no other edge inside
either class. The closed curve between them visits all
22 faces: a Hamiltonian cycle of G.

The exponent has a picture. Fix the lowest state and compare any other state with it. The two differ
along closed curves, and each white face gets the number of those curves that wind around it. That
number is its height. One clock move turns the wedges around a white face and raises that face by one.
The volume of a state is the sum of its heights, and the exponential sum weighs s by e to the volume
times x. So the analytic weights count white faces under a surface, and reversing a cycle of D changes
the volume by the number of white faces inside the cycle.

Once a state is good, its opposite edges forming one tree per root, no choices remain. Delete the chosen
spoke in every black face. What remains of the spoke graph is a spanning tree, so the curves that cross
the deleted spokes form a tree on the white faces. Root that tree at the white face next to the prescribed
edge e. Each tree edge runs past two sides of one black face, and the side facing away from the root of the
tree joins the selection. The selection, with e, splits the vertices of T into two classes that each induce a
tree. The boundary between the classes is one closed curve through every face. In G it is a Hamiltonian
cycle that avoids e.

Fix s and write a matrix with a row for each black face and a column for each non-root vertex. The row
of a face has two entries, at the ends of its opposite edge. Expanding the determinant picks one end in
every row and each column once, which is a partner r for s, so the determinant adds up the partners

two roots in one tree it is zero, as for five states here. This explains the cancellation, not why a good
state exists.

A state is a perfect matching between black centres and non-root vertices. Lay two states on top of each
other. Where they disagree, their spokes alternate around closed curves, and forgetting the centres turns
each curve into a cycle of D. Physicists call this a double-dimer picture, and a pair is the case with no
agreement, as in (a). The method is good at counting such overlays with a determinant. The trouble is
in (b). Two states that agree on some faces leave doubled spokes. A doubled spoke bounds no disk, the
disk identity has nothing to say about it, and the determinant counts these overlays together with the
pairs. So the standard tools count too much, and the surplus terms have no sign control.

A good state meets three conditions at once. Every black face has one wedge. Every non-root vertex is
used once. The edges opposite the wedges form three trees, one at each root. Each condition alone is a
matroid constraint, the third after the three roots are merged into one vertex. Matroid intersection, a
fast and standard method, meets any two of them together. The panels show what goes wrong when one
condition is dropped. The table counts the choices that pass each pair of tests, against the six that pass
all three. Intersecting three matroids is hard in general, which is why no algorithm falls out of the proof.
This does not show that finding a good state is hard.

Give each black face its own colour. Deleting a spoke of a face opens a passage between two white regions,
in the colour of that face. A good state is then a spanning tree on the white faces that uses every colour
once, with one passage at every non-root vertex. First find a spanning tree with one passage per vertex.

Three older ideas end at the same object. Stein showed that a Hamiltonian cycle of G is a split of the
vertices of T into two induced trees. Kelmans strengthened the conjecture to cycles that avoid or use a
prescribed edge, which makes gluing along small cuts possible. Feder and Subi colour the vertices of T,
contract one class, and look for a spanning tree of faces. A relaxed reading, tested in (c) and (d), asks
for an induced tree whose vertices outside one class are pairwise non-adjacent. Their theorem asks more,
a degree condition on omitted vertices. None of the three supplies the step from a pair to a good state.

and is unrefereed. An audit of this atlas found the 10-vertex example, recomputed here. Not read by a

ferent cycles. It does not reach every cycle. The hexagonal prism has eight Hamiltonian cycles. Four
of them avoid the prescribed edge, and the construction produces two. The test for a given cycle runs
the construction backwards. Orient the edges of T that the cycle does not cross towards the roots and
read off a state. The cycle is produced exactly when that state is good. The bottom row shows the four
states. Two are good. In the other two a path of opposite edges joins two roots. So counting good states
undercounts Hamiltonian cycles, and sampling good states does not sample cycles uniformly.

(c) Counts by direct enumeration, on a doubling scale. The number of good states stays at 2 in both families.
Counting on families shows how thin the set of good states can be. The dual of a prism with 2m sides
has m states and exactly two good states, while the number of Hamiltonian cycles of the prism grows
with m. A nanotube of width four is a stack of rings. Its states multiply with every layer, 2, 5, 13, 34,
and it still has exactly two good states. So the proof finds a cycle in a set of states where almost none
qualify, and the cycles it finds are a small part of all Hamiltonian cycles. Both families have no separating
triangles, so the rarity is not caused by gluing.

The paper extends the theorem to cubic bipartite graphs with a Pfaffian orientation by quoting a structure
theorem. A direct proof would rerun the argument on another surface. The smallest test is the Heawood
graph on a torus. Its dual is the complete graph on seven vertices. No roots are removed, since seven
black faces already match seven vertices. There are 24 states and 48 pairs, and every cycle of D runs
through all seven vertices. Such a cycle bounds no disk, the walk around it sees black faces on the left
seven times or once instead of three, and the two partners of each state cancel. The signed sum is zero.
The Heawood graph is Hamiltonian, so only the method fails.
