paper/draft-A/barnette.pdf.text:
HAMILTONIAN CYCLES FROM STATES
AN EXPOSITION OF OPENAI’S PROOF
Abstract. A spanning subgraph of degree two need not be a single cycle. We explain OpenAI’s proof
of Barnette’s conjecture by constructing a forest in the planar dual that forces the complementary
degree-two subgraph to be connected. Two disjoint face–vertex matchings encode the local choices. A
signed count cancels every cyclic choice, while heights at white faces show that the count is nonzero. The
surviving choice yields two induced trees with a prescribed facial pattern, which allows the construction
to pass across separating triangles.
1. Degree two and connectivity
A Hamiltonian cycle is a connected spanning subgraph of degree two. In a cubic graph, choosing
the omitted edge at each vertex is the easy part: the complement of a perfect matching has degree two
everywhere. Connectivity is the whole problem. On the cube, for instance, the two opposite square faces
give a spanning subgraph of degree two with two components.
We will enforce connectivity in the dual graph. There, omitted edges become a forest. Planarity turns
acyclicity of those edges into connectivity of their complement. The local degree condition and the global
connectivity condition then have separate certificates.
All graphs in the theorem are finite, simple and undirected. A graph is cubic if every vertex has degree
three, and is 3-vertex-connected if it has at least four vertices and remains connected after deleting any
two or fewer vertices.
Theorem 1 (OpenAI [10]). Let G be a cubic, bipartite, planar, 3-vertex-connected graph. For every edge
e of G, there is a Hamiltonian cycle avoiding e.
The edge prescription will let solutions on smaller pieces agree when we glue them. The proof below
explains OpenAI’s paired-state argument. Barnette’s conjecture was recorded in the 1969 Waterloo
proceedings [6].
Stein’s region-partition formulation [11, Theorem 2.2] led to the two-induced-tree
formulation given by Alt, Payne, Schmidt and Wood [1, Lemma 5]. The prescribed-edge strengthening
and the reduction to graphs without nontrivial three-edge cuts belong to the earlier work of Kelmans, as
explained by Hertel and by Alt et al. [7, 1].
Our main change is in the signed count. Li [9] replaces OpenAI’s exponential sum by involutions
on marked crossings. The constructive exposition [3] uses integer signs and a polynomial. The root-
component count below also follows that exposition. We use the product of face heights proposed in the
project note [4, Sections 1–3], and prove its counting identity here. We also use that note’s formulation of
the disk identity and its short recovery argument. The product of heights uses the same cancellation
mechanism, with each factor detecting enclosure of one face.
Fix a sphere embedding of G, drawn with piecewise linear edges, and let T = G∗be its dual. This is a
simple triangulation. Here are the details needed for simplicity. A cut of one or two edges in G would have
at least three vertices on either side: a singleton in a simple cubic graph has three outgoing edges and a
pair has at least four. Deleting the at most two cut endpoints on one side would therefore disconnect a
nonempty remainder, contrary to 3-connectivity. A loop or a pair of parallel edges in the dual would draw
a Jordan curve crossing just one or two primal edges, and would give such a cut. Cubicity now makes
every dual facial boundary a closed walk of length three in a simple graph, hence a triangle. Euler’s
formula gives |V (T)| = 2 + |V (G)|/2 ≥4. The bipartition of G colors the faces of T black and white,
with opposite colors across every edge.
We use the following elementary fact about duality. A spanning forest includes all vertices, with
isolated vertices allowed.
Date: November 14, 2026.
1
2
AN EXPOSITION OF OPENAI’S PROOF
Lemma 2. In a connected sphere graph, the edges complementary to a spanning tree dualize to a spanning
tree. The edges complementary to a spanning forest dualize to a connected spanning subgraph.
Proof. Contract the tree to one vertex. Faces are preserved, and its edges disappear from the dual. The
remaining dual is connected and has |E| −|V | + 1 = |F| −1 edges by Euler’s formula, so it is a tree.
Extend a forest to a spanning tree to obtain the second assertion.
□
Thus we want a forest P in T with exactly one side of each triangular face. Its complementary dual
has degree two because each triangle has two sides left, and is connected by Lemma 2.
For gluing, we will obtain this forest as two induced trees. For U ⊆V (T), the induced graph T[U]
contains every edge whose endpoints lie in U; a single vertex counts as a tree. If two induced trees
partition V (T), no triangle is monochromatic. Each triangle therefore has exactly one edge within a class,
as required. We prove the following precise dual statement.
Proposition 3. Let T be a simple sphere triangulation with at least four vertices and a proper black-
and-white face coloring. Given any facial triangle t0 and any side e0 of it, the vertices partition into two
induced trees such that the endpoints of e0 belong to one tree and the third corner of t0 belongs to the
other.
We first construct the partition when there is no separating triangle, meaning a 3-cycle with vertices
strictly on both sides. Section 6 then proves the proposition by induction. The matching and cancellation
arguments in between will also apply whenever a pair of states exists.
Example (The cube). Its dual is the octahedron. Use roots 0, 1, 2, other vertices 3, 4, 5, and the following
faces, written here as unordered vertex sets:
black
t0 = 012
t1 = 135
t2 = 234
t3 = 045
white
y0 = 015
y1 = 123
y2 = 024
y3 = 345.
We prescribe e0 = 01, so the eventual cube cycle must omit t0y0. The octahedron labels in Figure 1 are
these vertex labels. We will follow this example from states to the recovered cycle.
2. Local choices with a second state
Make t0 the outer face, and exchange the colors if needed so that it is black. Its three corners are the
roots R. If there are k black faces, side counting gives k white faces and 3k edges. Euler’s formula gives
k + 2 vertices. Consequently the bounded black faces A and the nonroot vertices X have the same size,
(1)
|A| = |X| = n = k −1,
|V (T)| = n + 3.
We need a local choice whose acyclicity can eventually be tested. Put a center ct in each black face
and join it to its corners by three spokes. We will delete one spoke at each bounded black center and
one at each nonroot. Such deletions are a perfect matching in the bipartite incidence graph B on A ∪X,
where t and v are adjacent when v is a corner of t. Equivalently, a state is a bijection s : A →X with
s(t) ∈V (t). These are Tutte states [12, 8]. We prove the state properties used below.
After deleting the spoke to s(t), the two remaining spokes join the other corners. Suppress the center
and replace that path by the opposite side of the triangle. Call the resulting spanning graph Qs. It
has one edge per face of A. Distinct black faces supply distinct edges, since an edge has only one black
incident face.
A forest Qs would be useful only if its components keep the three roots separate. A second state
supplies exactly this control. A pair (r, s) consists of states with r(t) ̸= s(t) at every t. If u(t) is the third
corner, orient the edge of Qs from r(t) to u(t). Every nonroot then has outdegree one, and every root
has outdegree zero.
Lemma 4. If s has a partner r, each component of Qs is either a tree with one root or a graph with a
unique cycle and no root. If Qs is a forest, it has three components, one at each root, and s has exactly
one partner.
Proof. In a component with v vertices and a roots, summing outdegrees gives v −a edges. Connectedness
gives at least v −1 edges, so a ≤1. For a = 1 the component is a tree; for a = 0 it has one cycle. In
a rooted tree all edges must point towards its root. In a rootless component all off-cycle edges point
towards the cycle, and the cycle has either of its two directions. These orientations determine the partner
by taking the tail in each black triangle. In particular the forest case gives a unique partner.
□

undirected simple cycle must be directed. Its edges require distinct tails, exhausting all its vertices.

unique same-label edge determines the prescription on the other piece. Apply induction there with the
cap as distinguished face and that edge as the prescribed edge. Rename the two labels to agree on the
common triangle.

Abstract. Barnette conjectured in 1969 that every cubic, bipartite, 3-connected planar graph has a
Hamiltonian cycle, and a 2026 preprint of OpenAI proves it. We give a self-contained account of that
proof in which every object is a set of edges or corners of one picture, the dual triangulation with its
faces coloured black and white. In that picture a Hamiltonian cycle avoiding a given edge is an acyclic
set of edges containing exactly one side of every triangle, and such a set can be built from a choice of one
corner in each black triangle whose opposite sides form a suitably rooted forest. To find such a choice
we count pairs of disjoint corner choices with signs: fixing the second choice cancels every pair whose
opposite sides contain a cycle, while grouping by the cycles along which the two choices differ shows
that the total is not zero. Both steps rest on one count, that a cycle of edges leaving chosen corners
encloses exactly one more white triangle than black. Separating triangles are removed by cutting and
gluing along the prescribed edge.
1. Introduction
A Hamiltonian cycle passes through every vertex of a graph exactly once. Barnette’s conjecture [3]
asserts that every cubic, bipartite, 3-connected planar graph has one. It belongs to a line of questions
that began with Tait’s 1884 conjecture that cubic 3-connected planar graphs are Hamiltonian [15].
Tutte disproved Tait’s conjecture in 1946 with a non-bipartite example [16], and Barnette asked whether
bipartiteness rescues it. For 57 years the conjecture was known only in special cases: when all faces have
four or six sides [7], under conditions on two of the three face colour classes [5], when all faces have at
most eight sides [13], and by computer for graphs with up to 90 vertices [10, 4]. In a preprint dated 24
September 2026, OpenAI proved it in the following stronger form [12].
Theorem 1.1. Let G be a finite simple graph that is cubic, bipartite, planar and 3-connected, and let e
be an edge of G. Then G has a Hamiltonian cycle that does not contain e.
The edge e is there for the induction in Section 6. Here a graph is 3-connected if it has at least four
vertices and stays connected after deleting any two of them. That the stronger statement is equivalent
to the conjecture was known before; see Hertel’s survey [8].
Degree two is easy; connectivity is the problem. In a cubic graph, deleting a perfect matching
leaves every vertex with exactly two edges, and cubic bipartite graphs have perfect matchings by Hall’s
theorem. So subgraphs in which every vertex has degree two are easy to find. Such a subgraph is a union
of disjoint cycles, and the whole difficulty is to make it a single cycle. Figure 1 shows both outcomes
on the graph we use as our example throughout. Every construction in this paper is there to enforce
connectivity.
The route. The proof turns connectivity into a counting problem in four steps, each forced by the one
before.
(1) Pass to the dual triangulation T. A perfect matching of G is a set of edges of T containing
exactly one side of every triangle, and its complement in G is connected exactly when this set
contains no cycle (Section 2).
(2) Fix a black triangle t0 with an edge e0. An acyclic set as in step 1 assigns to every other black
triangle one of its corners, using every vertex not on t0 once. Conversely, such a corner choice
yields an acyclic set whenever the sides opposite the chosen corners form a forest with one corner
of t0 in each component. Acyclicity comes from a single count. A cycle made of edges leaving
chosen corners encloses one more white triangle than black (Section 3).
(3) A second corner choice, disjoint from the first, orients the opposite sides and turns the condition
of step 2 into “no cycle”. Counting such pairs with a sign, the pairs that fail cancel in twos,
while a regrouping by the cycles along which the two choices differ shows that the total is not
zero (Section 4).

One picture. The three existing accounts of this proof [12, 11, 1] move between three graphs: the
primal graph G, its dual triangulation, and a graph of “spokes” joining the centre of each black triangle
to its corners. We tell the whole proof in the dual triangulation. Every object is a set of edges of T
or a set of corners of its black triangles. The graph G appears only as the graph of faces of T, in one
duality lemma that we use twice (Lemma 2.4). Spokes appear only as a way to draw a corner, when we
define heights in Section 4. In exchange, the four counts of the proof (the disk identity, the acyclicity of
the selected edges, the density bound for the first pair and the colour of a cap) become the same count:
Euler’s formula on a region of T, plus a count of edge sides by the colour of their face.
Sources. This is an exposition of OpenAI’s proof [12]. The objects (pairs of states, the opposite sides
Qs, the cycles D(r, s), the disk identity, the cancellation for a fixed second state, the regrouping by
cycles, the flow argument and the gluing) are all theirs. From Li [11] we take the point that the complex
exponential sum can be replaced by a finite signed count. From the constructive paper [1] we take the
real sign ε = (−1)(n+J)/2, the outdegree description of partners (our Lemma 4.2) and the formulation

unpublished notes written during a collaborative reading of the three papers; we checked each one and

• the disk identity in the form “one more white face than black” (Lemma 3.6);
• the short acyclicity proof of Proposition 3.7;
• the observation that every acyclic selection comes from a corner choice (Lemma 3.1);
• heights at white faces in place of the circulation lemma of [12], which removes the exponential
sum and the complex phase (Lemma 4.6);
• the finite-difference form of the nonvanishing argument (Lemma 4.7), which we apply to the

Two smaller changes are ours: we obtain the tree of faces Ys of Lemma 3.3 directly from Qs by duality in

replaces the sliding of edges onto spokes in [12, Section 5.3]. Tutte introduced the corner choices we call
states in his theory of trinity [17]; see also [9].

2. One picture
The dual triangulation. Fix an embedding of G in the sphere. Its dual T has a vertex in each face
of G and an edge crossing each edge of G once. Conversely G is the graph of faces of T: two faces are
adjacent when they share a side. Each face of T contains one vertex of G, and each edge of G crosses
exactly one edge of T.
Lemma 2.1. Let G be as in Theorem 1.1. Then T is a simple graph with at least four vertices, every
face of T is bounded by a triangle, and the faces of T can be coloured black and white so that every edge
of T has one black and one white face.
Proof. First, G has no set of at most two edges whose removal separates two nonempty vertex sets U
and V (G) \ U. A single vertex has three edges leaving it, and two vertices have at least four, so |U| ≥3
and |V (G) \U| ≥3. Deleting the at most two endpoints of the cut edges that lie in U leaves a nonempty
part of U with no edge to V (G) \ U, contradicting 3-connectivity.
A loop of T, or two edges of T joining the same two vertices, is a closed curve that meets G only
in one or two crossing points with edges of G. The two ends of a crossed edge lie on opposite sides of
the curve, so both sides contain vertices of G, and the crossed edges form a cut of size at most two.
Hence T is simple. The face of T containing a vertex v of G is bounded by a closed walk through the
three faces of G at v; in a simple graph a closed walk of length three is a triangle. Euler’s formula gives
|V (T)| = |F(G)| = 2 + |E(G)| −|V (G)| = 2 + |V (G)|/2 ≥4, since 3-connected graphs have at least four
vertices. Finally, colour the face of T containing v by the class of v in the bipartition of G. The two
faces at an edge of T contain the two ends of an edge of G, so they get different colours.
□
From now on T is a coloured triangulation: a simple graph with at least four vertices, embedded in
the sphere with every face a triangle, and with a black and white colouring of its faces such that every
edge has one face of each colour. Each edge has exactly one black face and each black face has three
sides, so the number of edges is three times the number of black faces, and likewise for white faces. With
Euler’s formula this gives

Definition 2.3. A selection is a set P of edges of T that contains exactly one side of every face of T.
We write P ∗for the set of edges of G crossing the edges of P.
A selection matches each black face with the white face across its selected side, so it has exactly k
edges. The question of the paper is which selections leave a connected graph in G. For a set S of edges
of a plane graph M, write M ∗−S∗for the spanning subgraph of the dual M∗whose edges cross the

Lemma 2.4 (duality). Let M be a connected simple plane graph and S ⊆E(M).
(1) If S contains a cycle Z, then the edges of M ∗joining a face inside Z to a face outside Z are
exactly those crossing Z, and M ∗−S∗is disconnected.
(2) If S is acyclic, then M ∗−S∗is connected. If S is a spanning tree of M, then M ∗−S∗is a
spanning tree of M ∗.
Proof. (1) By the Jordan curve theorem, Z splits the sphere into two open disks, and every face of M
lies in one of them. An edge of M ∗crosses only its own edge of M, so it joins faces on opposite sides
of Z exactly when it crosses an edge of Z. The two faces at an edge of Z lie on opposite sides, so both
sides contain faces. All edges of M ∗between the two sides cross edges of S, so they are missing from
M ∗−S∗.
(2) Suppose M ∗−S∗is disconnected, and let Φ be the set of faces in one of its components. Call an
edge of M a boundary edge if one of its faces is in Φ and the other is not. A boundary edge lies in S,

Proposition 2.5. Let P be an acyclic selection of a coloured triangulation T with dual G.
(1) The edges of G not in P ∗form a Hamiltonian cycle of G.
(2) P is a forest with exactly two components, and an edge of T lies in P exactly when its two ends
lie in the same component.
Proof. (1) Every face of T has exactly one side in P, so every vertex of G meets exactly one edge of
P ∗. Since G is cubic, the other edges give every vertex degree two. By Lemma 2.4(2) with M = T and
S = P, they form a connected graph, and a finite connected graph with all degrees two is a single cycle.
(2) P is acyclic with k edges on k + 2 vertices, so it has two components. Suppose an edge uv /∈P
has both ends in one component. Then P ∪{uv} contains a cycle Z through uv. By Lemma 2.4(1), the
edges of G crossing Z form an edge cut of G. The Hamiltonian cycle of part (1) meets this cut in exactly
one edge, the one crossing uv, because the other edges of Z are in P. But a cycle meets every edge cut
in an even number of edges.
□
Part (2) is Stein’s reformulation [14] in the form proved by Alt, Payne, Schmidt and Wood [2,
Lemma 5]: the two components are trees, and each contains every edge of T between its vertices.
A selection P containing an edge e0 of T gives a Hamiltonian cycle of G that avoids the edge of G
crossing e0. So Theorem 1.1 asks for an acyclic selection containing a prescribed edge. Figure 7 shows
one in the example; Section 3 constructs it.

Where the corner choices come from. Suppose P is an acyclic selection containing e0, and look at
P0 = P \ {e0}.
Lemma 3.1. Each of the three components of P0 contains exactly one root. Orient every edge of P0
towards the root of its component, and for t ∈A let s(t) be the tail of the side of t in P0. Then s is a
bijection from A to X, and s(t) is a corner of t for every t.
Proof. By Proposition 2.5(2), a and b lie in one component of P and c in the other, because ac /∈P.
Deleting e0 splits the first component into a part containing a and a part containing b. In a tree oriented
towards its root, every vertex other than the root has exactly one outgoing edge, so every vertex of X
is the tail of exactly one edge of P0, and the roots are tails of none. The side of t ∈A in P is not e0,
which lies in t0, so it lies in P0 and s(t) ∈X is defined. Distinct black faces have distinct selected sides,
since an edge has only one black face, and distinct edges of P0 have distinct tails, so s is injective. Every
x ∈X is the tail of an edge of P0, whose black face lies in A; so s is onto.
□
So the unknown in the problem is a choice of one corner in every face of A that uses every vertex of
X once.

4. Pairs of states
Why a second state. Goodness asks two things of Qs: no cycle, and one root per component. The
second condition is global and awkward to control. A second state takes care of it.
Definition 4.1. A pair is an ordered pair (r, s) of states with r(t) ̸= s(t) for every t ∈A; we call r a
partner of s. For a pair we write u(t) for the third corner of t.
Lemma 4.2. Let (r, s) be a pair, and direct the edge of Qs in each t ∈A from r(t) to u(t). Then every
vertex of X has outdegree one and every root has outdegree zero. Each component of Qs either is a tree
containing exactly one root, or contains no root and exactly one cycle, which is directed. In particular,
s is good if and only if Qs is acyclic.
